a: Titus Vespasian had been sent from Judea by his father
t: Titus on the road to Galba
p: Vespasian's older son left Judea to greet the new emperor, and a rumor said he was to be adopted.
b: Titus Flavius Vespasianus, called Titus Vespasian here, was the older of Vespasian's two sons and served under him in Judea. Tacitus says his father sent him to Galba. Suetonius tells the same trip: Titus was sent to congratulate Galba, people took him to be going for adoption, and he turned back when he saw new unrest in Rome (Titus 5). Tacitus adds the stop at Paphos (2:2-4), which Suetonius mentions in one line. Agrees in outline; Tacitus has the fuller account. This is not Paul's helper Titus (see the note on 2:86).

a: At Corinth, the main city of Achaia
p: Titus heard of Galba's death in the city where Paul worked and wrote.
b: Tacitus calls Corinth a city of Achaia (Latin urbs). The Latin has no word for "main" or "capital"; the Conversational English Translation adds "main". The New Testament knows the same city and the same province. Gallio "was serving as proconsul of Achaia" when the Jews led Paul before the judgment seat (Acts 18:12), and Paul had come to Corinth earlier (Acts 18:1). Paul wrote two letters to the church there (1 Corinthians 1:2; 2 Corinthians 1:1). Agrees: it is the same place, and Tacitus's phrase fits Acts. Titus passed through it in AD 69, in the years when Paul's churches were already established.

a: the prophecies that pointed his way
t: An old oracle from the East
p: Claude's theory: the 'prophecies' may include the belief that a ruler from Judea would rule the world.
b: Tacitus does not say which prophecies he means here. Elsewhere he says the Jews had a belief that in the ancient records of their priests "rulers, coming from Judea, were to acquire universal empire", and that these prophecies pointed to Vespasian and Titus (5:13, in Church and Brodribb's English). Suetonius (Vespasian 4.5) and Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.4, Whiston's numbering) tell of the same belief. Josephus calls the oracle ambiguous, says it was "found in their sacred writings", and says it meant Vespasian. None of the three names a verse. Claude's theory: the likeliest source in the Bible is "The scepter will not leave Judah" (Genesis 49:10) or "A star will march out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel" (Numbers 24:17). Christians read both of Jesus. The Romans took the oracle to point to their own general. Overlap with others: Josephus himself says the oracle came from the Jews' sacred writings and applies it to Vespasian. The Talmud (Gittin 56b, a story told centuries later) has Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai read Isaiah 10:34, about Lebanon falling to a mighty one, as a sign that Vespasian would be king. Neither source names Genesis 49:10 or Numbers 24:17, so those two verses are Claude's own guess.

a: to be adopted
t: Adoption: how a Roman got an heir
p: Emperors without sons named their heirs by adoption; Paul uses the same idea for what God does.
b: In Book 1 Galba adopts Piso and says a good successor is the best gift an old man can give the Roman people (1:15-16). That is why a rumor of adoption could make Titus a name in a day. Paul uses the idea for believers: "You received the Spirit of adoption as children" (Romans 8:15), and Christ came "so that we would receive adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). Background only: Tacitus and Paul do not know each other, but in the world of both, adoption could lift a person to the highest family.

a: Some believed he turned back because he longed for Queen Berenice
t: Queen Berenice: Titus, and Bernice in Acts
p: Tacitus's Berenice is very likely the Bernice at Paul's hearing; Josephus, not Acts, says she was Agrippa's sister.
b: Berenice was a Jewish queen of the Herod family. Josephus says she was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I (Antiquities 19.9.1) and calls Agrippa II her brother (Antiquities 20.7.3, Whiston's numbering). Acts spells her name Bernice: "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), and the two arrived "in grand display" at Paul's hearing (Acts 25:23; Acts 26:30). Acts does not say she was the king's sister; that comes from Josephus. Suetonius says Titus later sent her away from Rome (Titus 7). Verdict: very likely the same person. The name, the rank, the Herod family and the time all match, and Tacitus names her again beside Agrippa at 2:81. Acts never mentions her tie to Titus. Tacitus passes the story on as what "some believed" and says it did not hinder his business.

a: Rhodes and Cyprus
t: Titus's sea road is Paul's sea road
p: Titus sailed past the islands Rhodes and Cyprus that Paul's ship passed.
b: Titus coasted Achaia and Asia and made for Rhodes and Cyprus, then crossed to Syria. Luke records Paul's last voyage to Jerusalem along nearly the same lane: "The next day we reached Rhodes" (Acts 21:1), and then Cyprus "came into view, and we kept it on our left as we sailed on toward Syria" (Acts 21:3). Agrees in geography: this was the usual route between the Aegean and Syria. Nothing connects the two voyages except the road.

a: the temple of Venus at Paphos
t: Paphos: the shrine, and the town in Acts
p: Tacitus describes the goddess's temple at Paphos; Acts 13 names the town as home of a Roman governor and a magician.
b: Tacitus says Titus wanted to see the temple of Venus at Paphos, famous among locals and foreigners. Acts names the same town: Paul and Barnabas "went through the whole island as far as Paphos," where they met a Jewish magician named Bar-Jesus in the circle of the proconsul Sergius Paulus (Acts 13:6-7). When the magician set himself against them he was struck blind, and the proconsul "came to faith" (Acts 13:8-12). Agrees on the place. Acts does not mention the goddess's temple, and Tacitus does not mention Paul. The link is the town and a world full of priests who read signs.

a: the skill and craft of reading entrails
t: Haruspices: priests who read the entrails
p: Priests studied the insides of sacrificed animals to learn the gods' will; the Bible forbids such reading.
b: The Latin is scientiam artemque haruspicum, 'the skill and craft of the haruspices,' the diviners who studied the liver and other organs of a sacrificed animal. Tacitus says the craft came to Paphos with Tamiras of Cilicia, and that in time only the priest of Cinyras's family was consulted. The Bible knows the practice among other peoples: "The king of Babylon has halted where the road splits... He examines the liver" (Ezekiel 21:21). The Law bans it for Israel: no one may practice "divination, reads signs, looks for omens or works sorcery" (Deuteronomy 18:10). Tacitus reports it here without comment, and shows it again at 2:4 and 2:78.

a: It's a rounded mass that rises from a broad base to a narrow top, like a cone
t: A goddess shown as a stone
p: The cone-shaped image at Paphos was not a human figure; the Law bans standing stones.
b: Tacitus says the goddess's image was not human in form but a rounded mass rising to a point like a cone, and that the reason was unclear (set ratio in obscuro). The Bible knows sacred stones as well. Jacob set one up as a marker (Genesis 28:18), but the Law later banned them as Canaanite worship: "And do not set up a standing stone, which the LORD your God hates" (Deuteronomy 16:22). Only a parallel in kind: a sacred stone instead of a statue.

a: the Jewish war
t: The Jewish war and what Jesus said of Jerusalem
p: Tacitus says only Jerusalem remained; Jesus had spoken of its siege and fall.
b: In Tacitus's picture Vespasian had won nearly all of Judea and only the siege of Jerusalem remained. Luke records Jesus warning of that siege. He said: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). He also said the city "will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). He also said "not one stone will be left on a stone" (Luke 21:6). Agrees that a Roman army would surround Jerusalem; Tacitus is Roman history and says nothing of Jesus. Josephus tells the siege in Jewish War 5-6. Christians differ on how much of the Olivet Discourse this war fulfilled (see the topic page).

a: the mountain stronghold and the Jews' stubborn religion
p: Tacitus's word for the Jews' religion carries contempt; Acts uses a Greek word with the same double edge.
b: The Latin says the siege was hard ob ingenium montis et pervicaciam superstitionis, 'because of the nature of the mountain and the stubbornness of their superstition.' Superstitio was a Roman's word for religion that seemed excessive or foreign. The Conversational English Translation says 'religion' and keeps 'stubborn.' The Greek deisidaimonia shows the same range in the New Testament. Festus tells Agrippa the Jews had questions about "their own religion" (Acts 25:19), and Paul tells the Athenians they are "very devoted to the gods" (Acts 17:22). In Acts 25:19 Festus speaks neutrally. In Acts 17:22 the tone is debated: the word can be read as "very religious" or as "superstitious", and the Plain English Translation has "very devoted to the gods". In Tacitus the tone is sneering, and the same word reappears in his account of the Jews (5:13).

a: had given the same amount of vigor
t: A damaged word in the Latin
p: Fisher's Latin text marks 'labor' here as corrupt, so the sense of this clause is uncertain.
b: In the Latin, Mucianus's soldiers got their vigor from integra quies et inexperti belli †labor. Fisher's Oxford text puts a dagger (†) before labor, his mark for a word he thinks is corrupt. So the sense of this clause is uncertain. The sentence as a whole still sets Mucianus's rested army against Vespasian's tested one: Vespasian's men were hardened by dangers and hard work, and Mucianus's men by long quiet. The Conversational English Translation follows Church and Brodribb's "exemption from the hardships of war". See the variant entry for what the translation does if labor is wrong.

a: Mucianus commanded four in peacetime
p: Tacitus counts four legions in Syria and three in Judea; the numbers recur in his story.
b: A legion was a large unit of Roman citizen soldiers. Tacitus says Vespasian had three legions in Judea and Mucianus four in Syria (see also 1:10). At 2:6 he counts seven legions "in Syria and Judea," and at 2:76 Mucianus adds the two in Egypt to make nine. Book 5 names the three in Judea as the 5th, 10th and 15th (5:1, in Church and Brodribb). The legion that marched west with Mucianus is the 6th (2:83). The Gospels and Acts show the same army at small size: a centurion who says "I have soldiers under me" (Matthew 8:9) and a commander of a cohort in Jerusalem (Acts 21:31-32).

a: Mucianus governed Syria and Vespasian Judea
p: Syria and Judea were separate commands whose generals quarreled until Nero fell.
b: Syria was the large province next to Judea, with its capital at Antioch (2:79). The Gospels and Acts name earlier Roman governors of the region: Quirinius over Syria (Luke 2:2), Pilate over Judea (Luke 3:1), and later Felix and Festus (Acts 24-25). Vespasian was a general at war, not that kind of governor. Tacitus says the rivalry between him and Mucianus was set aside only when Nero fell, and Titus then joined them. Suetonius (Vespasian 6.4) also says Mucianus dropped his rivalry and put the Syrian army behind Vespasian. Agrees: both writers treat their partnership as the start of the Flavian cause.

a: The tribunes, the centurions and the rank-and-file soldiers
t: The Roman ranks in the Gospels and Acts
p: Centurions, tribunes and soldiers fill the New Testament, too.
b: Tacitus lists the ranks a general had to win over. The same ranks appear in the New Testament. A centurion asked Jesus to heal his servant and said "I am a man under someone's authority myself, and I have soldiers under me" (Matthew 8:9). Cornelius "was a centurion in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1), at Caesarea. The commander of the cohort in Jerusalem rescued Paul from the crowd (Acts 21:31-32). Background only: none of these men is in Tacitus, but they show the Roman army of Tacitus's years, in the same provinces, from the ground level.

a: Egypt with its two legions, and on the other side Cappadocia and Pontus
t: Provinces that are also Bible lands
p: Egypt, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia are all named in Acts and 1 Peter.
b: Tacitus lists the eastern provinces that could join a war: Syria and Judea, Egypt, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia. Several of these name the first Christian communities. The crowd at Pentecost came from "Mesopotamia, in Judea and Cappadocia, in Pontus and Asia... in Egypt" (Acts 2:9-10), and Peter writes to the Dispersion "in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1). Aquila, whom Paul met in Corinth, was "a man of Pontus by birth" (Acts 18:2). Background: a map of the East in AD 69 is also a map of the early church.

a: the huge, slow machinery of a civil war
t: Jesus on 'wars and reports of wars'
p: Jesus told his disciples to expect wars and not to panic; AD 69 was one such year.
b: Tacitus describes the East watching the West tear itself apart. Jesus told his disciples: "You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars. Take care not to panic. This has to happen, but the end is not here yet" (Matthew 24:6), and in Luke, "When you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified" (Luke 21:9). Many Christian readers see the Roman civil wars of AD 68-70, with the Jewish war inside them, as the first generation's experience of these words. Others read them of every age or of the end; the site's page on the Olivet Discourse sets out the readings. Tacitus's own verdict, "rich in disasters" (1:2), agrees with the facts, not with Jesus's meaning.

a: a report that Nero was on his way
t: The false Nero and the beast whose wound healed
p: Rumors that Nero lived and would return are a background for Revelation 13 and 17 in many readings.
b: Tacitus is an early witness to the rumor that Nero had not really died. He tells of a pretender, a slave or freedman who looked and sang like Nero, who was caught at Cythnus and killed. Some readers of Revelation connect this to the beast whose "death wound was healed" (Revelation 13:3), and to the beast "that was and is not," an eighth king who "belongs to the seven" (Revelation 17:11). Other readers think John's beast is the empire itself or an end-time ruler. Tacitus does not mention Christians here. The site's page on Nero sets out the views. Verdict on the link: a possible background, not a proven one.

a: to the Praetorians
p: The Praetorian Guard was the body of soldiers who guarded the emperor and Rome.
b: Praetoriani were the soldiers of the Praetorian Guard, the units that guarded the emperor in Rome. At this point Tacitus has them receiving a message from Syria: the centurion Sisenna was carrying the 'clasped right hands' token to them. Later Book 2 shows Otho's Guard beaten and Vitellius breaking it up and rebuilding it (2:67, 2:93-94). The Bible mentions them only in passing: Paul's chains were known "by the whole praetorium" (Philippians 1:13). The same Greek word, praitorion, means the governor's residence in Matthew 27:27, so which meaning Paul has is debated.

a: clasped right hands, the sign of friendship
p: Soldiers of Syria sent a token of clasped hands; Paul and the pillars of Jerusalem exchanged right hands.
b: The Latin says Sisenna carried dextras, concordiae insignia, 'right hands, the signs of concord,' a token to pledge the Syrian army's loyalty. Tacitus does not say what it looked like. The right hand was a common sign of agreement, and Paul uses it for the agreement at Jerusalem: James, Cephas and John "gave Barnabas and me their right hands in partnership" (Galatians 2:9). Only a custom in common.

a: Galatia and Pamphylia
p: Galba put one governor over Galatia and Pamphylia, lands Paul crossed on his journeys (Acts 13:13; 14:24; 16:6).
b: Tacitus says Galba gave Calpurnius Asprenas the government of Galatia and Pamphylia. These are lands Paul crossed on his journeys. From Paphos "Paul and the men with him put out to sea and reached Perga in Pamphylia" (Acts 13:13), and later "They crossed Pisidia and arrived in Pamphylia" (Acts 14:24). The Galatian country was also his (Acts 16:6). Agrees in place: the two names are the same lands. Tacitus shows how Rome governed them in AD 68-69, when the churches there were already a generation old.

a: 2,000 gladiators
t: Gladiators in the army, and in Paul's pictures
p: Otho's army included gladiators; Paul uses the arena for his own sufferings.
b: Tacitus calls them a disreputable help, yet even strict commanders had used them in civil wars before. Gladiators fought in public shows, and Rome used them as soldiers here (see also 2:23, 2:35 and 2:62). Paul draws on the arena for his own life. He writes: "God has put us apostles on show last of all, like people sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world" (1 Corinthians 4:9). He also says "I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus" (1 Corinthians 15:32). Background: Paul's readers knew these shows, and Tacitus's disgust at gladiators in an army fits the ordinary Roman view that the arena was low work.

a: Gallia Narbonensis
t: Southern Gaul, between Italy and Spain
p: Paul planned a trip to Spain; this province lay on the coast between Italy and Spain.
b: Gallia Narbonensis was the Roman province of southern Gaul, on the coast west of Italy and before Spain. It is not named in the Bible. Paul told the Romans of a plan "when I make my trip to Spain" (Romans 15:24). Background only: nothing in the New Testament mentions the province. Tacitus shows what a coast like this looked like in a civil war: armies burning and plundering as if abroad.

a: pointed to her womb
p: The Latin has her point to her womb; the older English says 'bosom.'
b: The Latin is uterum ostendens latere respondit, 'showing her womb, she answered that he was hiding there.' Church and Brodribb's 1864 English softens it to 'her bosom.' The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin. The sense is that the son was hidden where he came from. See the variant entry. A mother's courage under torture is a recurring story in Jewish writing too: the mother of the seven sons "watched seven sons perish within one day and bore it with a steady heart" (2 Maccabees 7:20). That is only a parallel in theme. The book is one that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles count as Scripture and Protestants do not.

a: Batavians
p: The Batavians fight for Vitellius here and rise against Rome in Book 4.
b: The Batavians were a people of the lower Rhine. In Book 2 they serve Vitellius and clash with the 14th legion (2:27, 2:66). Their revolt under Julius Civilis fills much of Book 4. The Bible does not name them. They matter here because they show how far the armies of AD 69 reached: Batavians from the Rhine fought on the Padus in Italy, while Vespasian's soldiers stood on the borders of Judea and the Euphrates.

a: a many-colored cloak and trousers, a foreign garment
p: To Romans, trousers were barbarian dress; Caecina wore them in towns that wore togas.
b: The Latin says Caecina wore a versicolor sagulus and bracae, 'a many-colored short cloak and trousers,' called a barbarian garment, while speaking to men in the toga. Bracae, 'trousers,' were Gaulish and German dress, and Tacitus takes the towns' offense for granted. His wife Salonina's purple riding dress also drew notice. Purple cloth was costly and marked rank: Lydia of Thyatira "sold purple cloth" (Acts 16:14) and soldiers put "a purple cloak" on Jesus to mock his kingship (John 19:2). Background: dress said who you were.

a: Bedriacum is a village between Verona and Cremona, and it has since become notorious for two great disasters for Rome
t: Bedriacum, the first battle and the second
p: The village gave its name to two battles in AD 69: Otho's defeat in April and Vitellius's in October.
b: Tacitus looks ahead to the two defeats at Bedriacum. Otho lost the first in mid-April AD 69, and Vitellius's army lost the second in October to the Danube armies backing Vespasian (told in Book 3). The Wikipedia article on the year gives 14 April for the first and 24 October for the second. Plutarch's Otho also tells the first battle, with the 21st legion (Rapax) and Otho's 1st (Adjutrix, Latin Adiutrix) fighting hardest (Otho 12.3), the same two legions Tacitus names at 2:43. Agrees.

a: Suetonius Paullinus and Marius Celsus
p: Suetonius Paullinus is a general; he is not the writer Suetonius.
b: Gaius Suetonius Paullinus, a former consul with a name for his campaigns in Britain (2:37), is a general in this book. He is not Suetonius the biographer, whose lives of the Caesars are used in these notes. Marius Celsus and Annius Gallus are Otho's other trusted commanders. Plutarch also shows Paullinus slow to help the cavalry at the ambush and urging Otho to wait for the Moesian troops (Otho 7.3, 8.2-4), which matches Tacitus's picture of him as slow and careful (2:25, 2:32).

a: King Epiphanes
p: A king named Epiphanes fought for Otho; he may be the son of King Antiochus of Commagene.
b: Tacitus names only 'King Epiphanes,' wounded as he fought hard for Otho. Josephus names an Antiochus Epiphanes at Jerusalem, a warlike son of the king of Commagene who came with armed men to help Titus (Jewish War 5.11.3), and later says the king of Commagene had a son Epiphanes (Jewish War 7.7.1). Tacitus calls the father Antiochus "the richest of the subject kings" at 2:81. Tacitus does not give this king's land or father. Verdict: possible that it is the same man. Josephus's Epiphanes is a son of a king; Tacitus does not say whose son his Epiphanes is.

a: Vitellius's whole army has already arrived
p: Paullinus argues that time favors Otho: supplies, the weather and reinforcements from the Danube.
b: Tacitus gives Suetonius Paullinus a long speech for delay: Vitellius's army has no grain, the Germans will wilt in the summer heat, the 14th legion and the Moesian troops are coming, and Italy, Rome and the East stand behind Otho. Plutarch gives Paullinus the same advice, to wait for the Moesian forces (Otho 8.2-4), but only in indirect speech. Suetonius says Otho chose to fight quickly either because he could not bear the continued worry and hoped to end the war before Vitellius came, or because he could not resist his soldiers, who clamored for the fight (Otho 9). Agrees in substance. Tacitus writes the speech in direct words, and Suetonius gives no speech.

a: withdrawing to Brixellum
p: Otho stayed back at Brixellum, a town on the south bank of the Padus; the tomb Plutarch saw was there.
b: Tacitus says Otho's brother Titianus and the Praetorian prefect Proculus talked him into leaving the army to save himself "for the highest matters and for ruling," and that this day first crushed his cause. Suetonius agrees that Otho stayed back at Brixellum and lost the decisive battle without him (Otho 9). Plutarch spells it Brixillum and says he saw Otho's modest tomb there, with the words "To the memory of Marcus Otho" (Otho 18.1). Agrees; Tacitus and Plutarch also agree that the tomb was plain (2:49).

a: Flavius Sabinus, the consul-elect
p: Otho sent a consul-elect named Flavius Sabinus to command troops; Vespasian's brother of the same name was prefect of the city.
b: Tacitus names two different men Flavius Sabinus in Book 2. At 2:36 Otho sends "Flavius Sabinus, the consul-elect" to command the troops Macer had led. The Wikipedia article on this consul of AD 69 says Gavin Townend identified him as Vespasian's nephew, a son of the elder Sabinus, and that other scholars have accepted this (the article names Brian W. Jones). At 2:55 Tacitus names Flavius Sabinus as prefect of the city. That man is Vespasian's elder brother. Plutarch says Otho appointed "Flavius Sabinus, a brother of Vespasian" prefect of the city (Otho 5), and Book 3 says Sabinus "was the elder" (3:65, in Church and Brodribb). The brother is the one who took the Capitol later that year with the cohorts that kept watch by night. Josephus tells that Vitellius's soldiers took the hill, brought Sabinus to Vitellius and killed him, and set the temple on fire (Jewish War 4.11.4, Whiston's numbering). Suetonius says Vitellius drove Sabinus and the Flavians into the Capitol and set fire to the temple of Jupiter (Vitellius 15). Agrees on the brother's end, and Book 3 tells it in full.

a: I find in some authors
p: Some authors said the armies hesitated; Plutarch has talk of peace after the defeat.
b: Tacitus reports a claim he does not share: that the two armies, sick of both emperors, might have talked peace or let the Senate choose. Plutarch has a related scene after Bedriacum, where Celsus and Annius Gallus persuade the officers to seek peace and Titianus first favors an embassy (Otho 13.2-3). Partly agrees: peace talk happened after the defeat, but Plutarch does not describe a plan before it. Tacitus's own reply (2:37-38) is that people who loved war would not suddenly love peace.

a: The old, long-planted human craving for power
p: Tacitus traces civil war to a craving for power; James traces wars to cravings inside people.
b: Tacitus names a human craving, old and planted deep, that grows with the empire's power. He follows it from Marius and Sulla to Pompey and the two emperors of AD 69. James asks the same question and answers it from the heart: "Where do the wars among you come from, and where do the fights come from? Is it not from here, from your cravings for pleasure that wage war in your body's members?" (James 4:1), and "You want and do not have. You murder and you envy" (James 4:2). Agrees in diagnosis. The Christian reading adds that the craving is sin and the cure is a new heart, which Tacitus cannot offer.

a: Gnaeus Pompeius
p: Tacitus lists Pompey among the men who turned Roman freedom into one-man rule; he also took Jerusalem in 63 BC.
b: Pompey (Gnaeus Pompeius) is named here as a man who 'hid his character better but was no better.' In Book 5 Tacitus calls him "the first Roman to conquer the Jews" (5:9, in this site's translation) and says he entered the temple. The topic page on Rome gives his capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC. The Bible does not name him. Link: a Roman general who shaped Judea's history is judged here only on the Roman side.

a: the 21st, called the Rapax
p: Legions had numbers and nicknames; the Rapax (Vitellius) and the Adjutrix (Otho) fight face to face.
b: A legion carried a number and, often, a nickname. The Latin Rapax means 'grasping'; Adiutrix means 'helper' (the translation writes Adjutrix). The 21st (Rapax) fought for Vitellius, and the 1st (Adjutrix), new to battle, for Otho. In the fight the 1st took the eagle of the 21st, the legion's sacred standard, and the 21st then drove the 1st back (2:43). Plutarch also says these two legions fought hardest (Otho 12.3). Both legions are named again in the marching order at 2:100. Agrees with Plutarch.

a: putting too high a price on my life
p: Tacitus and Plutarch give Otho the same thought: better to die than to prolong a civil war.
b: In Tacitus, Otho says he will not let more young Romans be cut down for him, and that blaming gods or men is for someone who wants to live. Plutarch has him tell the soldiers that the day was more blessed than the day they made him emperor and that he could die with more honor than he could reign over a war against fellow Romans (Otho 15.4-6). Agrees in meaning. Neither writer was there, and the wording is the author's. Tacitus has Otho add a note of dynasty pride: he was the first to bring the throne into a new family (2:48).

a: he fell on the blade with his chest
t: Suicide in the Bible, and Otho
p: Saul fell on his sword; Otho does the same, and the writers praise him.
b: Tacitus, Suetonius and Plutarch all say Otho killed himself with a dagger at dawn, after drinking water and sleeping (Suetonius, Otho 11; Plutarch, Otho 17). The Bible tells of a few deaths by a person's own hand or request. Saul asked his armor-bearer to stab him, and when he refused, "Saul took hold of the sword and fell on it" (1 Samuel 31:4). Abimelech asked to be finished off so no one could say a woman killed him (Judges 9:54). Ahithophel hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). Zimri burned the king's house down over himself (1 Kings 16:18). Judas "went and hanged himself" (Matthew 27:5). Samson pulled a building down on himself and the Philistines: "The dead he killed in his death outnumbered those he had killed in his life" (Judges 16:30). Hebrews names Samson among those of faith (Hebrews 11:32), and many readers count his death as an act of war, not suicide, as the site's topic page on suicide says. Differs in the verdict: Tacitus calls Otho's end the best act of his life (2:50), while none of the Bible accounts states a verdict on the act itself. Christians differ on how to speak of suicide; see the topic page.

a: Some of the soldiers killed themselves beside the funeral pyre
p: Suetonius also says several soldiers killed themselves by Otho's body.
b: Tacitus says some soldiers killed themselves at the pyre, "not from guilt or fear, but out of rivalry for his glory and love of their emperor," and that the habit spread at Bedriacum, Placentia and other camps. Suetonius agrees that several soldiers killed themselves beside the bier, and that others far away did the same (Otho 12). Plutarch also says some soldiers died at the pyre (Otho 17-18). Agrees among all three.

a: a bird of an unfamiliar kind
t: A strange bird at Regium Lepidum
p: Tacitus keeps his distance from this omen: local people told it, and he will not reject it.
b: Tacitus says marvels and made-up tales are beneath his work, but he will not discredit what "common report and tradition" say. The locals told of an unfamiliar bird in a busy grove near Regium Lepidum that stayed until Otho died. Plutarch and Suetonius give other omens before Otho's reign, such as a statue turning east (Plutarch, Otho 4.4-5) and delays from Tiber floods and bad omens (Suetonius, Otho 7-8). Jesus warned that an evil generation "keeps hunting for a sign" (Matthew 12:39); the Bible's own signs come from God and have a purpose. Only a contrast.

a: honored Asiaticus with the rings
p: A gold ring marked a Roman Knight; James describes a man with gold on his fingers.
b: The army wanted Vitellius to make his freedman Asiaticus a Roman Knight, and he first refused, then gave him the rings at a private dinner. The gold ring was the badge of knight's rank. Suetonius says Vitellius freed, sold and restored Asiaticus, then gave him the golden ring (Vitellius 12). James pictures the same mark of rank in a church: "Say a man with gold on his fingers and bright clothes walks into your synagogue, and a poor man in dirty clothes walks in as well" (James 2:2). Only background: a ring told everyone where a person stood.

a: the champion of Gaul and a god
t: A man who claimed to be a god
p: Mariccus claimed to be a god; Acts shows others who took such titles or were hailed as gods.
b: Mariccus, a commoner of the Boii, called himself the champion of Gaul and a god and gathered 8,000 men. Acts records people hailed or claiming to be great. Simon in Samaria is one, of whom the people said, "This man is the Power of God" (Acts 8:10). Theudas "said he was someone important" (Acts 5:36). Herod Agrippa I heard the crowd cry "It's a god speaking, not a man!" (Acts 12:22). Jesus warned of "false messiahs and false prophets" who would give signs (Mark 13:22). Only a pattern in the first century: the claim to a divine rank could gather a following, and Rome treated it as revolt.

a: thrown to wild beasts
t: Beasts that did not harm him?
p: The crowd thought Mariccus was invulnerable because the animals did not tear him; Daniel's rescue had another cause.
b: Tacitus says Mariccus was thrown to wild beasts, did not get torn, and the "foolish crowd" believed him unhurtable, until he was killed in front of Vitellius. Daniel's story has the same detail with another meaning: the king found Daniel unharmed, and Daniel said his God had sent his angel (Daniel 6:22). Differs: in Tacitus, the beasts that do not attack him are taken as proof of a divine man and are then answered by the sword; in Daniel, the rescue was God's act and was no human claim. Tacitus does not say why the animals held back.

a: The astrologers were driven out of Italy
t: Astrologers expelled, and magicians in Acts
p: Vitellius banned astrologers from Italy; Acts shows magicians in the courts of Roman officials.
b: The Latin is pulsi Italia mathematici: 'the mathematici,' the astrologers, were driven out of Italy. Suetonius says Vitellius hated them, ordered them out of Rome and Italy, and that a mocking placard answered his edict (Vitellius 14). Astrologers still turned up around the next emperor (2:78 names Vespasian's own, Seleucus). The Bible knows such diviners: Babylon's advisers who "map out the sky" and "stare at the stars" (Isaiah 47:13) and the "magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers and the Chaldeans" of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:2). In Acts Sergius Paulus kept a magician, Bar-Jesus, in his circle (Acts 13:6-7), and in Ephesus believers burned their magic books (Acts 19:19). Agrees that such men advised the powerful.

a: refused the name of Caesar
p: 'Caesar' and 'Augustus' were titles of the emperor, as in Luke and Acts.
b: Vitellius put off the title Augustus and refused the name Caesar, but kept all his real power (2:90 shows the crowd pushing him to take Augustus). Both were already the emperor's titles. Luke dates Jesus's birth by "Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1) and John the Baptist's preaching by "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1). Paul, on trial, says "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11), and Festus's words about the "emperor" render the Greek Sebastos, 'Augustus' (Acts 25:21). Agrees: the titles mean what they mean in Tacitus.
orig: vocabulum Augusti differret, Caesaris non reciperet

a: thousands of unburied citizens
p: To leave the dead unburied was a disgrace in Roman and biblical eyes; Vitellius is not moved.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius did not look away or shudder at the many thousands left unburied, and instead made a sacrifice to the gods of the place. Suetonius says Vitellius urged his men not to mind the smell of the dead (Vitellius 10). In the Bible, burial is a duty and its lack a mark of judgment: "The corpses of your servants they have handed to the birds of the sky to eat... and there was nobody to bury them" (Psalm 79:2-3), and in Jeremiah, "No one will mourn them, and no one will bury them" (Jeremiah 16:4). Agrees that unburied dead mean disaster; Tacitus's point is the emperor's cold heart.

a: crowds of eunuchs
p: Tacitus lists eunuchs among the habits of Nero's court that Vitellius copied.
b: Eunuchs, castrated men who served in royal courts, travel with Vitellius as part of 'the habits of Nero's court.' The Bible knows them in Eastern courts and in the early church: the Ethiopian official whom Philip met was a eunuch (Acts 8:27). Suetonius says Vitellius made offerings to Nero's memory and urged musicians to play Nero's songs (Vitellius 11). Only background: a eunuch at court meant power and money in many cultures, as the site's topic on eunuchs shows.

a: a runaway slave named Geta
p: A runaway slave posed as a noble; Paul's letter sends Onesimus back to Philemon, and whether he was a runaway is disputed.
b: A man claimed to be Scribonianus Camerinus, a nobleman believed to have hidden in Histria, and gathered a crowd. His owner recognized him as a runaway slave named Geta, and he was punished 'the way slaves are.' In Philemon, Paul writes about Onesimus and says "I am returning him to you" (Philemon 1:12). The traditional reading is that Onesimus was a runaway. The letter does not say so; Philemon 1:15 says only that "he was parted for a short time". Allen Dwight Callahan has argued against the runaway reading (Harvard Theological Review, 1993, as Wikipedia's article on the letter reports), and that article also lists scholars who defend it. On either reading, Paul asks Philemon to receive him "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 1:16). Differs: Geta is punished; Onesimus is sent back with a plea for kindness. Only background: both cases involve a slave and the claims of a master.

a: Tiberius Alexander, the prefect of Egypt
t: Tiberius Alexander: a Jew by birth who governed Egypt
p: The prefect of Egypt was a Jew by birth and had once governed Judea.
b: Tiberius Julius Alexander was born into a rich Jewish family of Alexandria. According to the Wikipedia article, his uncle was the philosopher Philo, he governed Judea about AD 46-48, and he was prefect of Egypt from 66. Josephus says Claudius sent Cuspius Fadus to be procurator of Judea, "and after him Tiberius Alexander" (Jewish War 2.11.6, Whiston's numbering). Josephus also says he "did not continue in the religion of his country" (Antiquities 20.5.2). The traditional reading is that he left Judaism. The Wikipedia article says some recent scholars think Josephus meant only that he took service with Rome. Tacitus says he made the legions swear to Vespasian on 1 July (2:79), and Suetonius gives the same day (Vespasian 6.3). Tacitus calls him a native of Egypt (1:11). The Bible does not name him. Link: a Jew by birth who ruled Judea for Rome belongs to the same world as the Herod family and the Roman governors in the Gospels and Acts. Verdict on any match with a New Testament name: none found.

a: at sixty, with his two young sons
p: Suetonius gives Vespasian's birth date, which makes him almost sixty in AD 69.
b: Suetonius says Vespasian was born on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December (17 November), five years before Augustus died, and died aged 69 years, 7 months and 7 days (Vespasian 2.1, 24.1, with the editor's note). That puts his birth in AD 9 and his sixtieth year at AD 69, which agrees with Tacitus. His two sons are Titus and Domitian, both young. Agrees. The dates work out from Augustus's death in AD 14.

a: That was how Scribonianus was killed under Claudius
t: Murder as a way to the throne
p: Vespasian fears one assassin more than armies; Tacitus recalls an earlier case under Claudius.
b: Vespasian thinks a single killer can end a campaign: under Claudius, Tacitus says, Scribonianus was killed and his killer Volaginius rose from the ranks to the highest military post. Tacitus does not explain the case further here. The Bible too tells of kings murdered by their own officials, such as Joash (2 Kings 12:20-21). Only a pattern: those closest to a ruler were his nearest danger.

a: who, after many private talks, now also spoke before them all
t: Mucianus's speech: a Roman set piece
p: Tacitus gives Mucianus a long speech; Josephus and Suetonius say Mucianus backed Vespasian but give no speech.
b: Mucianus's speech to Vespasian is the pivot of Book 2: he argues that the throne helps the state, brings glory and is within reach, that Vitellius is a weak rival, and that the East has nine legions. Josephus has Mucianus and the other commanders urging Vespasian on, after the soldiers proclaimed him (Jewish War 4.10, Whiston's numbering), and Suetonius has Mucianus put aside his old rivalry and promise the Syrian army (Vespasian 6.4). Neither gives a speech, so the wording is Tacitus's. Partly agrees: Mucianus did push him, but Josephus puts the soldiers' shout first and Mucianus second. Tacitus has Mucianus move first, then the shout (2:80). The Wikipedia article on Mucianus, citing Gwyn Morgan (2006), has Mucianus persuade Vespasian at a meeting on Mount Carmel in May or June 69 (see the note on 2:78).

a: the divine Augustus
p: Mucianus calls Augustus 'divine': Roman emperors were made gods after death.
b: Mucianus says 'the divine Augustus,' a title the Senate gave to dead emperors who were voted a place among the gods. The living emperor was honored in a lesser way. Luke names "Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1) without the title. The New Testament treats such honors as a danger. When the crowd shouted of Herod Agrippa I, "It's a god speaking, not a man!" (Acts 12:22), "an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God" (Acts 12:23). Link: the site's page on ruler worship traces how the cult grew.

a: Have you forgotten Corbulo's murder?
p: Corbulo was a famous general whose murder Mucianus recalls as a warning to Vespasian.
b: Tacitus has Mucianus ask, "Have you forgotten Corbulo's murder?" and argue that a well-known man is never safe under a ruler who fears him: anyone who is feared is famous enough to the one who fears him. Tacitus gives no more on Corbulo's death here.

a: nine fresh legions from Judea, Syria and Egypt
p: Three in Judea, four in Syria, two in Egypt: nine.
b: The nine legions are the three in Judea, the four in Syria and the two in Egypt, which Tacitus has counted at 2:4 and 2:6. According to the Wikipedia article on Mucianus, which cites Gwyn Morgan, the army that marched west with him was the 6th legion (Ferrata) and detachments of 2,600 men from each of the five other legions of Syria and Judea. Tacitus himself says the 6th legion and 13,000 men from the detachments followed at 2:83; the figure of 2,600 from each legion is the article's. Agrees: 5 x 2,600 is 13,000.

a: A cypress on his land
t: The cypress that fell and rose again
p: A tree that fell and sprouted again fits Bible pictures of a royal tree cut down and restored.
b: Tacitus says a tall cypress on Vespasian's land suddenly fell and next day rose from the same spot, taller and broader and green, and the diviners called it a great sign. Suetonius gives the same omen but places the cypress on Vespasian's grandfather's farm, uprooted in calm weather, and says it sprouted greener and stronger (Vespasian 5.4). Agrees in the main event; the two differ on whose land. The Bible has a close picture. It is Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a tree cut down with its stump left, which Daniel explains as meaning "your kingdom will stay yours, once you know that Heaven rules" (Daniel 4:26). Job also speaks of a tree that will "come back with new growth" (Job 14:7). Josephus says Daniel "also wrote concerning the Roman government, and that our country should be made desolate by them" (Antiquities 10.11.7, Whiston's numbering), but that passage does not mention the cypress. Only a parallel: Tacitus does not connect the omen to Daniel, and Suetonius does not either.

a: an astrologer named Seleucus
p: Suetonius says an astrologer named Seleucus also advised Otho; the same man is possible.
b: Tacitus says that later, as master of the world, Vespasian openly kept an astrologer named Seleucus as his adviser and forecaster. Suetonius says that an astrologer Seleucus had told Otho he would outlive Nero (Otho 4; the editor's note there says Tacitus and Plutarch name Ptolemaeus for this part of the story). Verdict: possible that this is one man who served both, since the name and the trade match. Neither writer says so.

a: Between Judea and Syria is Carmel
p: Tacitus's Carmel is the mountain of Elijah's contest, now with a god and an altar of its own.
b: Carmel is the mountain where Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal: "How long will you limp along on two crutches? If the LORD is the God, go after him. If Baal is, go after him" (1 Kings 18:21). Tacitus puts it between Judea and Syria and says the name belongs to both the mountain and the god. The Wikipedia article on Mount Carmel reports a Greek inscription "To Heliopolitan Zeus of Carmel" (published by Avi-Yonah, 1952). It says Carmel was a major center for the storm god Hadad, whom it also calls Baal, and that Avi-Yonah and other scholars argue that the Baal Elijah defeated was Hadad (1 Kings 18:19-40). Suetonius says Vespasian consulted the oracle of the god of Carmel (Vespasian 5.6). The Wikipedia article on Mucianus, citing Gwyn Morgan (2006), dates a meeting of the commanders at Carmel in May or June 69, at which Mucianus persuaded Vespasian to take up arms. That would put Carmel in the middle of the story Tacitus tells. Agrees on place and on a holy mountain; a Christian reader notes that the contest on Carmel showed which god is the God (1 Kings 18:39).

a: the god has no statue or temple, only an altar and reverence
t: An altar without a statue: Elijah's altar remembered?
p: Claude's theory: a Carmel altar with no image could be the memory of the altar Elijah mended.
b: Tacitus says the ancestors of the locals handed down that the god of Carmel has no image and no temple, only an altar. Elijah "mended the LORD's altar, which had been knocked down" and built an altar of twelve stones "in the LORD's name" (1 Kings 18:30-32), and the God of Israel is not shown by an image. Claude's theory: the bare altar of Tacitus's report could be an echo of this, by way of local memory. Against it: the inscription to Zeus of Carmel in the Wikipedia article shows a Greek-style god worshiped on the mountain, and Tacitus says nothing of Elijah or Israel. Overlap with scholarship: the Wikipedia article on Mount Carmel notes only that a monastery altar there is claimed to be Elijah's, which it calls unlikely. That is a later tradition and says nothing about Tacitus, so the link from Tacitus's altar to Elijah's is Claude's own. Verdict: possible, unproven.

a: the priest Basilides
p: Tacitus's Basilides is a priest at Carmel; a Basilides also appears at Alexandria in Book 4.
b: At Carmel the priest Basilides examines the entrails and tells Vespasian he will get a great dwelling and many men. In Book 4 a Basilides, "one of the chief men of Egypt", appears to Vespasian in the temple of Serapis at Alexandria though he is days away (4:82, in Church and Brodribb). Suetonius gives that vision to his freedman Basilides (Vespasian 7.1). Kenneth Scott (Journal of Roman Studies 24, 1934) suggests, on the first page of his article, that Tiberius Alexander, the prefect of Egypt, had a representative, "a certain Basilides", in these dealings. The same page speaks of a conference held with Mucianus at Mount Carmel. Tacitus does not link the priest at Carmel to the Basilides of Egypt. Verdict: possible but unproven that the priest and the Egyptian are one man; the places are far apart.

a: you're being given a great dwelling, huge boundaries, and many men
p: Suetonius says the oracle of Carmel promised success in whatever Vespasian planned.
b: In Tacitus, the priest's answer is a riddle about a house, fields and slaves, which rumor then spelled out as the throne. Suetonius says the oracle of the god of Carmel gave Vespasian lots that promised whatever he was planning would succeed (Vespasian 5.6). Agrees in meaning and differs in form: one has a spoken riddle, the other lots. Josephus tells his own story of prediction: that he foretold the throne to Vespasian and was freed (Jewish War 4.10; Suetonius, Vespasian 5.6).

a: The move to hand the empire to Vespasian began in Alexandria
p: Alexandria is Apollos's home city and the home port of two ships that carried Paul (Acts 27:6; 28:11).
b: Alexandria, in Egypt, was the second city of the Mediterranean world. Acts mentions Alexandrians in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), the learned Apollos, "an Alexandrian by birth" (Acts 18:24), and two ships "out of Alexandria" that carried Paul toward Rome (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11). Tacitus says Tiberius Alexander made the legions swear to Vespasian on July 1st, which Vespasian later counted as the first day of his reign. Suetonius gives the same day (Vespasian 6.3). Josephus puts the oath after Vespasian wrote to Tiberius Alexander (Jewish War 4.10.6, Whiston's numbering). Agrees on the place.

a: Mucianus for Antioch
p: Tacitus's Antioch is the city where the disciples were first called Christians.
b: Tacitus calls Antioch the capital of Syria. Acts tells of the same city: "Antioch was the first place where the disciples came to be called 'Christians'" (Acts 11:26), and its church sent out Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1-4). Agrees: the same city. Mucianus rallies the province there (2:80) and mints coin there (2:82). Josephus says Vespasian came to Antioch to give out offices (Jewish War 4.11.1, in Whiston's numbering).

a: Vespasian for Caesarea
t: Caesarea, capital of Judea in Acts
p: Tacitus calls Caesarea the capital of Judea; Acts has Cornelius, Felix and Agrippa all there.
b: Caesarea on the coast is where the Roman governors lived. Acts has the centurion Cornelius "in Caesarea" (Acts 10:1) and Herod Agrippa I going "down to Caesarea" (Acts 12:19). Paul is sent there under escort to Felix, the governor (Acts 23:23-24). King Agrippa also "came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13). Josephus says Vespasian returned to Caesarea after finishing the places around Jerusalem (Jewish War 4.10). Agrees: same city, same role.

a: July 1st
t: Two dates for the first oath
p: Tacitus and Suetonius give 1 July at Alexandria; Josephus tells the order the other way.
b: Tacitus says Tiberius Alexander had the legions swear to Vespasian on July 1st, and that this was later celebrated as the first day of his reign, though the army of Judea swore on July 3rd. Suetonius also says the legions in Egypt swore first on 1 July and that Judea followed (Vespasian 6.3). His editor's note says that his reckoning for Judea (five days before the Ides) gives July 11 against Tacitus's July 3 (see the variant entry). Josephus writes that the soldiers in Judea proclaimed Vespasian first, and that Vespasian then wrote to Tiberius Alexander for his support (Jewish War 4.10, Whiston's numbering). A footnote in Whiston's translation says Vespasian was first saluted emperor in Judea, and suggests that the month Tacitus and Suetonius give for the Judean oath was meant to be June, not July. Differs: which came first, Alexandria or Judea.

a: hailed him as emperor
t: How Vespasian became emperor: Tacitus and Josephus
p: In Tacitus a few soldiers greet him as emperor and he stays calm; in Josephus the troops threaten him until he accepts.
b: Tacitus says that one day a few soldiers waiting to greet him as legate hailed him emperor, the rest piled on the names Caesar and Augustus, and Vespasian was not swollen or changed. Josephus has the soldiers gather and proclaim him emperor, and says Vespasian at first refused and accepted only when they threatened him with drawn swords (Jewish War 4.10). Differs in the refusal: Tacitus has none. In both, the army chose him before any formal act of the Senate. The word the soldiers used was imperator, 'commander,' from which our word 'emperor' comes.

a: the theater at Antioch
t: A city's assembly in a theater
p: In the East, crowds met in the theater to hear leaders; Acts shows the same at Ephesus.
b: Tacitus says the people of Antioch customarily held their discussions in the theater, and that Mucianus spoke there. Acts has the same custom at Ephesus: after the silversmiths' riot "the people charged into the theater" (Acts 19:29), and Paul was kept from going "before the people's assembly" (Acts 19:30). Agrees as to custom. Mucianus's speech here sells the army a rumor that Vitellius would swap the German and Syrian legions.

a: He was fairly polished even in Greek
p: The East spoke Greek; the Roman commander in Jerusalem asks Paul, 'You know Greek?'
b: Tacitus notes that Mucianus spoke well even in Greek, which an eastern audience would expect. The commander who arrested Paul in Jerusalem asked him, "You know Greek?" (Acts 21:37), and Paul answered in Greek before turning to Aramaic. Only background: a Roman officer's Greek was never taken for granted by the Greek-speaking East.

a: Sohemus joined with his kingdom
p: Three client kings, Sohemus, Antiochus and Agrippa, join Vespasian; Josephus knows them too.
b: Rome ruled the East partly through client kings. Tacitus names Sohemus, who 'joined with his kingdom,' Antiochus (the king of Commagene, whom Tacitus calls the richest of the subject kings; the Wikipedia article on him cites this very verse), and Agrippa. Tacitus says nothing more about Sohemus here. Josephus names Antiochus's son Epiphanes among Titus's helpers at Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.11.3). Of the three, only Agrippa is in the New Testament.

a: Agrippa, called away from Rome by secret messages from his people
p: This Agrippa is Agrippa II, the king before whom Paul spoke in Acts 25 and 26.
b: Agrippa II was a king of the Herod family. Josephus says Herod Agrippa I (whose death is told in Acts 12) left a son Agrippa, then seventeen, and three daughters, one of them Bernice (Antiquities 19.9.1, Whiston's numbering). Acts shows the younger Agrippa with Festus: "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), where Paul spoke before him (Acts 26). Tacitus has him in Rome in AD 69 and hurrying home to join Vespasian. Verdict: very likely the same man: same name, same title, same period, and Josephus gives him a sister Bernice. Acts itself does not say they were brother and sister; that comes from Josephus. The Wikipedia article on Berenice says Agrippa and she shared power.

a: Queen Berenice backed the cause
t: Berenice: Vespasian's ally and Paul's Bernice
p: Tacitus says Berenice, pleasing to old Vespasian by her gifts, backed him; the same woman sat at Paul's hearing.
b: Tacitus says Berenice backed Vespasian 'with no less spirit,' in the bloom of youth and beauty, and pleased the old man by the magnificence of her gifts. See the note on 2:2 for her place in Acts ("Bernice," Acts 25:13, 25:23, 26:30). Her sister Drusilla is also in Acts: "Felix came with Drusilla, his own wife, a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24). Josephus lists Drusilla among the daughters of Agrippa I (Antiquities 19.9.1) and says Felix married her (Antiquities 20.7.2). Verdict: very likely the same woman as the Bernice of Acts.

a: A council on the whole conduct of the war was held at Berytus
t: Berytus: the council before the march
p: Mucianus and Vespasian's captains met at Berytus (modern Beirut) to plan the war.
b: Berytus was a coastal city of Syria, now Beirut. Tacitus says Mucianus came there with his legates, tribunes and best soldiers, and that picked men from the Judean army came too, with kings competing in display. Josephus also has Vespasian go to Berytus, where Mucianus reported the oaths taken across the province, and Josephus says he freed Josephus at about that time (Jewish War 4.10). Tacitus gives no month for the council; he says only that Syria's whole army had sworn before July 15th. The Wikipedia article on Mucianus puts the council in July. Agrees. The Bible does not name Berytus.

a: At Antioch gold and silver were coined
p: Tacitus says the war was paid for with coin struck at Antioch; Jesus once asked whose image was on a coin.
b: Money mattered to every army (2:84). Jesus asked for a coin and asked, "Whose image is this, and whose name is written here?" and they answered, "Caesar's" (Matthew 22:20-21). Only background: the coin of the Gospels was the emperor's, and an emperor in the making needed his own.

a: Envoys went to Parthia and Armenia
p: Vespasian's side secured the eastern border; Suetonius says the Parthian king offered archers.
b: Parthia was the great empire east of Syria. Suetonius says its king Vologaesus promised 40,000 archers (Vespasian 6.4); Tacitus says only that envoys went so the legions' backs would not be left bare. Parthians appear among the Pentecost crowd in Acts 2:9. Agrees.

a: Titus would press on in Judea
p: Tacitus says Titus was to press on in Judea; Josephus says Vespasian sent him from Alexandria after Vitellius fell.
b: Tacitus has the plan made now: Titus stays to finish Judea, Vespasian holds Egypt. Josephus puts the order later: after Vitellius died, Vespasian, still in Alexandria, sent Titus with picked forces to destroy Jerusalem, and Titus marched through Gaza, Ascalon, Joppa and Caesarea (Jewish War 4.656-663). Partly agrees: both have Titus take the siege. Luke records Jesus's warning of what the siege would bring (Luke 21:20-24).

a: Informers were everywhere, and the richest men were picked out for plunder
p: Mucianus used informers to gather money; Jezebel did the same to Naboth.
b: Tacitus says Mucianus judged by the size of a man's wealth and that informers were everywhere. The nearest Bible case is Naboth, framed so that Jezebel could take his vineyard: she told the elders to "Put two worthless men across from him, and have them testify against him" (1 Kings 21:10). Only a parallel in method: charges used to seize property. Tacitus does not say any of Mucianus's victims were framed; he says rich men were chosen.

a: pulled the soldiers of Dalmatia along
p: Dalmatia is where Paul's helper Titus went; he is not the emperor's son.
b: Dalmatia is the Roman province along the Adriatic. 2 Timothy 4:10 says that "Titus" went "to Dalmatia", and earlier that he preached "as far as Illyricum" (Romans 15:19). The Titus of 2 Timothy is Paul's co-worker. Verdict: unlikely to be the same man as Vespasian's son, who was a general in Judea and later emperor; the name Titus was common. The Dalmatia of Tacitus is a war zone in AD 69, with Pompeius Silvanus as governor.

a: buffoons, actors and charioteers
t: The circus crowd, and Paul's racecourse
p: Vitellius surrounded himself with entertainers; Paul uses the racecourse as a picture of discipline.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius took pleasure in buffoons, actors and charioteers, whom he knew from low services, and brought them along. Chariot races and games filled Roman life (see the stable and circus shows at 2:94). Paul assumes his readers know the racecourse: "on a race course everyone runs, but only one gets the prize" (1 Corinthians 9:24), and the athlete's "crown that fades" (1 Corinthians 9:25). Only background: Paul turns a pastime that Tacitus finds shameful in an emperor into a lesson in self-control.

a: he went up to the Capitol
t: The Capitol and the temple at Jerusalem
p: Vitellius goes up to the temple of Jupiter; a few months later it burned, and Jerusalem's temple fell in AD 70.
b: The Capitol was Rome's holy hill, with the temple of Jupiter. It was burned in the fighting between Vitellius's soldiers and Flavius Sabinus, just before Vitellius fell (Josephus, Jewish War 4.11.4; Suetonius, Vitellius 15; told in Book 3). The Jerusalem temple fell in AD 70. Jesus had said of it, "days will come when not one stone will be left on a stone. Every one will be knocked down" (Luke 21:6). Link: the two great temples of the empire were destroyed within about a year of each other. Tacitus does not say this; it is a pattern the reader sees.

a: a day marked since ancient times as unlucky
t: An unlucky day and the day of Haman's lot
p: Romans marked July 18 as unlucky; Haman had a lot cast to choose a day.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius's notice for a public ceremony on July 18 was taken as a bad omen, because that day was long marked by the disasters at the Cremera and the Allia. Suetonius says Vitellius took the chief priest's office "on the day of Allia" (Vitellius 11), and his editor notes it was a day of special ill omen because of the defeat by the Gauls in 390 BC. In Esther, Haman had a lot cast to pick the day for his plan against the Jews: "Pur, that is, the lot, was thrown before Haman, day by day and month by month" (Esther 3:7). The book says that on the day set for it, the plan "was turned upside down" (Esther 9:1). The Plain English Translation of Esther never names God in that verse or anywhere else in the book. Jewish and Christian readers have read that silence as God's hidden hand, which is a reading, not the text. Only a parallel: both worlds read days as signs.

a: once he became chief priest
t: 'Chief priest' in Rome and in Jerusalem
p: The Latin is 'greatest pontiff,' the emperor's priestly office, not the high priest of Jerusalem.
b: The Latin is maximum pontificatum, the office of pontifex maximus, head of the Roman priests. The Conversational English Translation says 'chief priest' and avoids 'high priest' so that no one confuses it with the high priest of Jerusalem. The Greek Gospels call the Jerusalem high priests archiereis, 'chief priests,' which English Bibles also render 'chief priests' (John 19:15). The two offices are unrelated, though both had charge of a state's worship.

a: The freedmen of earlier emperors were ordered to contribute like a tax
p: Vitellius taxed his predecessors' freedmen by the number of their slaves; Jesus told people to pay what is Caesar's.
b: Having no money for the soldiers' bonus, Vitellius ordered the freedmen of earlier emperors to pay, in proportion to the number of their slaves. Taxes under the emperors are all through the New Testament. Luke dates Jesus's birth by a registration ordered by Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:1). Jesus answered about the coin, "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Matthew 22:21). Paul tells believers to submit to authorities (Romans 13:1). Background only: Tacitus shows how an emperor under pressure raised money.

a: holding funeral rites for Nero
p: Suetonius also says Vitellius made offerings to Nero at the Campus Martius.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius built altars on the Campus Martius and held funeral rites for Nero, with animals sacrificed and burned and the Augustales lighting the fire. Suetonius agrees that Vitellius made offerings to Nero in the Campus Martius and at the banquet cheered Nero's songs (Vitellius 11). Agrees. For Nero in the Bible world see the topic on Nero.

a: the Augustales lit the fire
t: The Augustales: priests of the emperor's house
p: The Augustales were a priesthood of the Julian family, set up by Tiberius, says Tacitus.
b: Tacitus says the Augustales were a priesthood that Tiberius Caesar dedicated to the Julian family, as Romulus did one for King Tatius. Luke names this emperor: "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1). Link: the emperor's priesthood is part of the cult of the ruler that the New Testament meets in Acts and Revelation (see the topic on ruler worship).

a: Rome, great and wretched
t: Rome, Babylon and the seven kings
p: Many Christian readers see Rome as the 'Babylon' of Revelation and the emperors as its kings.
b: Tacitus says Rome had put up with an Otho and a Vitellius in one year. Revelation 17 names "Babylon the Great" (Revelation 17:5), a woman who sits on seven mountains, which are also "seven kings. Five have fallen. One is. The other has not yet come" (Revelation 17:9-10). Peter sends greetings from "her who is in Babylon" (1 Peter 5:13). Many readers take Babylon to be Rome. Readers differ on the count of kings and on which emperor is the sixth; the site's pages on Rome and Nero set out the views. Possible link, not proven: Tacitus does not mention Christians or Revelation.

a: the Etesian winds
p: Summer winds helped ships sail east and blocked those sailing back; Luke's ships met such winds.
b: Tacitus says the sea with the Etesian winds favored those sailing east but not those coming back, so Vespasian's letters moved slowly toward Rome. Acts shows how winds ruled sailing: "we kept to the sheltered side of Cyprus, since the winds were blowing against us" (Acts 27:4), and "going on by sea had become risky, since the Fast was already past" (Acts 27:9). Agrees in spirit: ancient sailors did not cross open water against the season.

a: the advice of Flavius Sabinus, with Rubrius Gallus carrying the messages
p: Tacitus says Caecina was approached by Vespasian's brother; Josephus says Caecina went over near Cremona.
b: Tacitus says Caecina's mind was shaken by the advice of Flavius Sabinus, with Rubrius Gallus carrying messages, and also by hatred of Valens and by greed for a place in the new reign. Josephus has Caecina see Antonius Primus's strong force near Cremona and then persuade his officers to go over to Vespasian; the soldiers regretted it that night and chained him (Jewish War 4.11.2-3, Whiston's numbering). Partly agrees: both have the betrayal and the mutiny. Tacitus gives the private motive, Josephus the battlefield one.

a: The writers of the time, who set down the records of this war while the Flavian house held power
t: Who wrote under the Flavians? Josephus
p: Claude's theory: Tacitus's complaint about flattering writers could include Josephus, who was freed by Vespasian.
b: Tacitus says that the writers who recorded this war while the Flavian house was in power wrote of 'concern for peace and love of the state' to flatter. He names none of them here. Josephus wrote the Jewish War, which tells these same months, after Vespasian had freed him (Jewish War 4.10). Claude's theory: Tacitus's charge fits Josephus as well as any Roman author, but Tacitus does not name him. Overlap with scholarship: Josephus himself says Vespasian freed him as a man who had foretold the throne (Jewish War 4.10), and Suetonius says the same (Vespasian 5.6). That is why a link is easy to draw, but neither source, nor Tacitus, makes the link to this sentence. Verdict: possible. The point for the reader is that Tacitus knew his sources wrote with a bias and says so.
